The conversation with Chris is on my Substack. Today at 11:30 AM ET, immigration attorney and military law expert Margaret Stock joins me on the legal architecture of veteran deportation and military spouse arrests.
Link: austinkocher.substack.com/p/… 
Link: austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

I'll be honest, this conversation was part interview, part counseling session for me. I haven't always known what to do with my veteran identity in relation to this work. Chris helped me think through it in ways that were meaningful.

The Chamberlain Network is also tracking in real time: military installations used for detention, Guard deployments for civilian law enforcement, and the constitutional questions those decisions raise. That tracker is at chamberlainnetwork.us.

Chris founded the Chamberlain Network to train veterans for civic life, not as partisans, but as people with a specific skill set and the moral authority to defend the institutions they once wore a uniform to protect.

Chris deployed to Iraq in 2011. His gun truck crew: an Ethiopian refugee, an Egyptian-American, a country boy from West Virginia, and the son of an Irish immigrant from Belfast. He said: "I really saw America captured in the people there."

Veterans and immigrants share more than most people realize. My conversation with @ChamberlainVets founder Chris Purdy changed how I think about both and about my own identity as a veteran doing immigration research.

Veterans For Good: Keeping America's Promise to Immigrants Who Served

You're invited to live discussions with Margaret D. Stock (Cascadia Cross Border Law Group) today at 11:30 AM ET

I wrote more about why I'm speaking up now, what my own service taught me, and what I still got wrong. Full essay here and I'd especially value hearing from other veterans. 

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

I also want to be explicit: my invitation to discuss this extends to veterans whose conclusions differ from mine. What I want is the actual range of veteran thinking, not the version ventriloquized by politicians who never served.

What I've learned: there's a growing international network of organizations (Repatriate Our Patriots, the Deported Veterans Support House in Tijuana, #AfghanEvac) doing work I should have known about years ago. I'm playing catch-up, and I want to share what I'm learning.

Military service, when honestly entered into, is a form of sacrifice this country has long called sacred. The threshold for what is owed in return has to be correspondingly high. Arrest, detention, and deportation cannot clear that bar, for any veteran.

The short answer is that the current targeting of veterans is an acceleration of a much older bipartisan failure. The legal architecture that makes a noncitizen veteran deportable was built across multiple administrations and left in place by successive Congresses.

I started boot camp in summer 1999 at 17 years old. I earned an honorable discharge before I turned 22. I study immigration enforcement for a living. I still didn't understand how badly our system treats veteran families until this past year.

I published the full dataset and analysis in March. Sharing it again now because the numbers keep growing and the pattern holds. Full post here: 
austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

This is the through-line connecting everything I'm covering this week with veterans and veteran-led organizations. The system that killed Paktiawal is the same system that deports veterans and abandons our Afghan allies. It is one story.

Paktiawal survived the Taliban. He did not survive ICE. @ShawnJVanDiver and @AfghanEvac said it plainly at the time: "We are not going to let Nazeer's death be in vain." I believe them. The question is whether the rest of us are paying attention.

I wrote this analysis in 2022. I'm sharing it now because the structural argument holds and because understanding how we got here matters for understanding what it will actually take to fix it. Full post: austinkocher.substack.com/p/bidens-off...

The legal framework that makes a noncitizen veteran deportable wasn't built by this administration. It was built across multiple administrations and left in place by successive Congresses. That's the bipartisan failure I keep coming back to.

I wrote then that it was hard to see any underlying principle guiding Biden's immigration policies. Four years later, that structural incoherence: over-promising, under-delivering, leaving legal architecture intact, is directly relevant to where we are now.

Berks County detention center in Pennsylvania had been emptied of detainees in March 2021. Less than a year later, ICE was filling it back up. The reduction of detention populations was temporary. The infrastructure never went away.

By February 2022, USCIS had approved just 160 Afghan humanitarian parole requests from overseas while denying 930 out of 40,000 filed. That 85% denial rate came from the administration of the president who promised to be the opposite of Trump on immigration.

Immigration detention didn't become a crisis in 2025. I wrote this in February 2022: the Biden administration was defending indefinite detention before the Supreme Court, reopening Berks County detention center, and denying 85% of Afghan parole applications.
